analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal estate tax owed on the largest inheritances.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill drew 183 House cosponsors but never got a committee vote, sitting at Ways and Means since its February 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the federal estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, the two taxes owed when very large fortunes pass to heirs. It keeps the gift tax but rewrites it so a person could give away $10 million during life tax-free, with anything above that taxed at rates topping out at 35% — far below the current 40% top estate tax rate. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the very largest estates. The estate tax already applies only to estates above roughly $14 million per person ($28 million per married couple), which is a tiny fraction of all estates — so repeal wipes out tax bills worth millions exclusively for the wealthiest families. Very large family farms and closely held businesses also gain, though the current exemption already shields nearly all of them.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate tax for anyone dying on or after the day the bill becomes law [S2].
Repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth skips a generation (for example, straight to grandchildren) [S2].
Keeps the gift tax but cuts its top rate to 35% and sets a $10 million lifetime tax-free gifting allowance, letting large fortunes be passed during life at far lower cost than under current law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses the revenue the estate tax raises — revenue that comes exclusively from multimillion-dollar inheritances. That money either has to be replaced with other taxes, borrowed, or dropped from the budget, so the cost is spread to everyone else.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate tax eliminates a tax paid only by the largest inheritances, so the lost revenue would have to come from somewhere — broader taxes or more federal debt [S2].

The bill keeps a gift tax but rewrites it with a $10 million lifetime exemption and a 35% top rate, so the wealthiest families could still move huge sums to heirs during life far more cheaply than under current law [S2].

Supporters' main concern — that the tax forces families to sell farms or businesses — is largely addressed by today's high exemption, which already protects virtually all farms and small businesses; repeal mainly relieves the very largest fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain goes to a small number of very wealthy families each year, while the lost revenue is spread across everyone else. The bill is a large, targeted tax cut for the top sliver of estates, and it also loosens the gift tax so wealth can be shifted during life at a discount — a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2025 and has sat there with no committee vote and no floor action ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Feenstra introduced the bill on February 13, 2025 [S1].
It attracted 183 cosponsors — 180 Republicans and 3 Democrats [S3].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no further action has been taken since [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax remains on the books, so the Treasury keeps the revenue that repeal would have given away — revenue that otherwise would have been replaced by taxes on a broader base or more borrowing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; the estate tax remains in place

for.name: Rep. Randy Feenstra
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 183 cosponsors for it.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill's referral; no committee markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — 180 of 223 House Republicans signed on versus 3 of 217 House Democrats — and the committee never acted.

industries.note: The estate tax applies only to estates above roughly $14 million per person, so repeal wipes out tax bills worth millions exclusively for the largest fortunes. The lost revenue would otherwise reduce deficits or other taxes borne by everyone else.

industries.industry: Family farms and closely held businesses
industries.note: Only the very largest farm and business estates benefit, since the current exemption already shields nearly all of them from the tax. Repeal removes the remaining estate-planning burden on large family operations.
Repeal shrinks the demand for complex estate-tax planning, though the reworked gift tax preserves some of that work.

analysis.trajectory: Full repeal is unlikely this Congress. Congress instead raised the estate tax exemption to $15 million per person in the 2025 tax law, which removed much of the urgency behind repeal; the bill will probably remain in committee without a vote.
